items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Economic crisis was the most important reason for the emergence of authoritarian states in the inter-war period."
items.answer: Economic crisis was a powerful catalyst, but authoritarian leaders came to power only where political systems were weak and elites collaborated.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Depression and Nazi vote rise 1930–1932; biennio rosso and Fascist support; GMD hyperinflation 1947–1949. Arguments against: weak democratic institutions (PR, Article 48); impact of war and the Versailles settlement; role of elites (Hindenburg, Victor Emmanuel III); ideological appeal and leadership. Supported judgement: Economic crisis was a powerful catalyst, but authoritarian leaders came to power only where political systems were weak and elites collaborated.

items.answer: Mass unemployment, business failures and farm debt discredited the Weimar parties; the Nazis offered work, national revival and a scapegoat, and their vote rose from 18% (1930) to 37% (1932).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "stab-in-the-back myth"?
options: The false claim that the German army had not been defeated in 1918 but betrayed by socialists, Jews and politicians at home
Extremely rapid inflation that destroys the value of money, as in Germany in 1923 when a US dollar was worth over 4 trillion marks
The clause of the Weimar Constitution that allowed the president to rule by emergency decree, used heavily by Chancellor Brüning in 1930–1932
Living space; Hitler’s aim of conquering territory in eastern Europe for German settlement

An historian is researching the economic conditions that helped authoritarian leaders gain power. Explain the value and limitations of Source B for this research, with reference to its origin, purpose and content.
items.answer: Value: A leading historian of Nazi Germany using statistical electoral research; gives a detailed, evidence-based interpretation. Limitations: It is a synthesis of other research, and electoral statistics cannot reveal individual motives.

items.stem:
Source A: Paraphrased from Denis Mack Smith, British historian, Mussolini, 1981

It was not the strength of fascism but the weakness of the liberal state that made Mussolini’s success possible. The liberal elites thought they could use him to restore order and then discard him.

Source B: Paraphrased from Paul von Hindenburg, former Chief of the General Staff, testimony to a Reichstag committee of inquiry, 18 November 1919

The army was not defeated in the field; it was stabbed in the back. Where the blame lies is clearly proved. If any further proof were needed, it lies in the statement of the British general that the German army was stabbed in the back.

Using the sources and your own knowledge, to what extent do you agree that the weakness of democratic systems was more important than economic crisis in the rise of authoritarian states?
items.answer: Weak systems were a necessary condition and economic crisis the catalyst; the two worked together.

items.stem:
Source A: Benito Mussolini and Giovanni Gentile, “The Doctrine of Fascism”, Enciclopedia Italiana, 1932 (extract, translation)

Anti-individualistic, the Fascist conception of life stresses the importance of the State and accepts the individual only in so far as his interests coincide with those of the State. For the Fascist, everything is in the State, and nothing human or spiritual exists, much less has value, outside the State.

Source B: Mao Zedong, Report on an Investigation of the Peasant Movement in Hunan, March 1927 (extract, translation)

A revolution is not a dinner party. A revolution is an insurrection, an act of violence by which one class overthrows another.

In what ways do Sources A and B agree and disagree about the ideologies of fascism, Nazism and communism?
items.answer: Both reject liberal individualism. Mussolini stresses the supremacy of the state over the individual, while Mao stresses class struggle and violence by one class against another; Fascism focuses on national unity, Maoism on class conflict.
items.markingKey: Both reject liberal individualism. Mussolini stresses the supremacy of the state over the individual, while Mao stresses class struggle and violence by one class against another; Fascism focuses on national unity, Maoism on class conflict. items.stem: State what is meant by the term "Great Depression".
items.answer: The world economic slump that followed the Wall Street Crash of October 1929, causing mass unemployment and the collapse of trade
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the world economic slump that followed the Wall Street Crash of October 1929, causing mass unemployment and the collapse of trade. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The false claim that the German army had not been defeated in 1918 but betrayed by socialists, Jews and politicians at home"?
items.answer: stab-in-the-back myth
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of stab-in-the-back myth.

items.stem: Distinguish between Italian Fascism and German Nazism.
items.answer: Both were ultra-nationalist and anti-communist, but Nazism made racial antisemitism and Lebensraum central, while Fascism focused on the state and the corporate economy.
items.markingKey: Both were ultra-nationalist and anti-communist, but Nazism made racial antisemitism and Lebensraum central, while Fascism focused on the state and the corporate economy. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Lukas writes: "Hitler came to power because the Nazis won a majority of votes in a free election." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The Nazis never won a majority in a free election (37.3% at their peak); Hitler was appointed chancellor by Hindenburg on 30 January 1933 after backroom intrigue.
items.markingKey: The Nazis never won a majority in a free election (37.3% at their peak); Hitler was appointed chancellor by Hindenburg on 30 January 1933 after backroom intrigue. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the Weimar Constitution was vulnerable to authoritarian challenge.
items.answer: Proportional representation produced fragmented coalitions, Article 48 allowed rule by decree, and elites in the army, judiciary and civil service remained hostile to the Republic.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Proportional representation produced fragmented coalitions, Article 48 allowed rule by decree, and elites in the army, judiciary and civil service remained hostile to the Republic. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Mao applied Marxism exactly as Marx had described it." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Marx expected revolution in industrial societies led by the proletariat; Mao adapted it to rural China, relying on peasant armies and guerrilla war.
items.markingKey: Marx expected revolution in industrial societies led by the proletariat; Mao adapted it to rural China, relying on peasant armies and guerrilla war. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the impact of hyperinflation in 1923 and the impact of the Depression after 1929.
items.answer: Hyperinflation ruined savers but the Republic survived, helped by the Dawes Plan; the Depression caused mass unemployment and political polarisation that brought the Nazis to power.
items.markingKey: Hyperinflation ruined savers but the Republic survived, helped by the Dawes Plan; the Depression caused mass unemployment and political polarisation that brought the Nazis to power. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which the May Fourth Movement of 1919 shows the link between national humiliation and new political movements.
items.answer: Students in Beijing protested against the Versailles decision to give Germany’s Shandong rights to Japan. It stimulated radical nationalism and Marxism, leading to the founding of the CCP in 1921.
